How much foreign exposure passes through domestic firms?
A non-importer can still depend heavily on foreign inputs through domestic suppliers. Allowing links to change is especially important for larger counterfactual trade shocks.
Domestic procurement is not itself an exposure metric. Buyers need to distinguish supplier location from imported-input dependence.
Network reconstruction could help when links are missing, but the paper relies on observed administrative transactions rather than LLM-inferred relationships.
Alfaro–Chor shows direct sourcing shifts; this paper explains why indirect links change their interpretation.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
My short version
A firm can be strongly exposed to foreign inputs even if it never imports directly. It may buy from domestic firms that import, or from their customers. The paper makes this indirect exposure visible with Belgian transaction data. It also shows why letting buyer–supplier links change matters more for large trade shocks than for small ones (PDF pp. 2–5, 41).

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
How the paper gets there
Domestic VAT transactions are linked to customs/intra-EU trade records and annual accounts. The authors first study a fixed network and then allow supplier choices with link-specific fixed costs. To keep network formation tractable, eligible suppliers follow an ordering that produces an acyclic network. They estimate the model and compare foreign-price counterfactuals. The large-shock results are model-based exercises, not observed impacts of a particular tariff announcement.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
This is a foundation for questioning “domestic sourcing” as a resilience metric. For an OM project I would ask how a buyer should choose among domestic suppliers with different hidden imported-input content. A feasible first model might use bounds on upstream exposure rather than require complete tier-2 data. The practical decision would be allocation across suppliers, and the performance measure would be expected cost plus shortage risk.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
VAT and customs microdata are not ordinary public downloads. The acyclic approximation helps computation but is still a modeling restriction. A sourcing change that looks optimal after a shock also may require qualification time absent from a static comparison. I should distinguish an exposure-accounting project from an optimization contribution.

title: Trade and Domestic Production Networks
text:
Questions for Yannis
Could partial information about indirect imports be sufficient for a useful sourcing rule? What access would we realistically have to firm-to-firm transaction data, and what could be done if it is unavailable?

Who bears tariffs, and how are gains and losses distributed?
In the 2018 episode, import buyers bore substantial duty-inclusive costs. Gross buyer losses, producer gains, tariff revenue and net real-income effects are different objects.
Buyers facing policy uncertainty can front-load inventory, wait, qualify alternatives or reserve capacity. These actions create a link from trade policy to operating performance.
No AI causal result. AI tools could help scenario analysis, but policy regime shifts challenge models trained on old data.
Caliendo–Parro is a quantitative tariff/welfare benchmark; Niu studies actual sourcing restructuring; Jain links sourcing to inventory.
Can I use the estimated pass-through for today's tariffs?
Only as evidence from that episode. Pass-through depends on product markets, time horizon and adjustment. I would not assume the 2018 estimate is a universal 2026 parameter.
The consulted version's $51bn gross loss and $7.2bn net loss are not interchangeable; the net estimate is statistically uncertain.

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
My short version
The central result I need is about who pays for tariffs. In the 2018 episode studied here, the authors find essentially complete pass-through into duty-inclusive import prices. That means domestic buyers of imports bear substantial costs; the foreign exporter does not simply absorb the tariff. The small net aggregate estimate also hides much larger transfers and uneven regional effects (PDF pp. 2–5).

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors use product–origin tariff variation to estimate trade-demand and export-supply responses, with event-study and pre-trend checks. They then combine the estimates with a supply-side model for aggregate and regional calculations. In this version, the $51 billion import-buyer loss is a gross component, while the $7.2 billion aggregate real-income loss is net of producer gains and tariff revenue. These are different quantities. The net estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels once parameter uncertainty is considered.

title: The Return to Protectionism
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
This motivates a buyer-level problem about tariff uncertainty and inventory. A buyer can front-load orders, wait, qualify an alternative or reserve capacity. I would ask when a temporary buffer dominates costly supplier replacement, given uncertain policy duration and long replenishment lead times. The paper establishes that costs matter; it does not solve that operational decision.

title: The Return to Protectionism
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
These are short-run results for the 2018 tariffs, not a universal pass-through parameter for every product in 2026. Country-time and product-time controls also remove some broader price movements. Treating tariffs as instruments requires assumptions; political targeting is a reason to inspect identification carefully.

title: The Return to Protectionism
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can an empirical project connect pre-announcement exposure to inventory and supplier-switching responses? How could we distinguish tariff avoidance from demand changes and routine seasonal ordering?

Why can a small shock destroy productive supply relationships?
I see the key change as treating the network itself as a choice. Relationship-specific gains and bargaining can make privately chosen links disappear in a cascade, even when an efficient allocation would adjust continuously.
Supplier retention, purchase commitments and relationship investment connect individual operating decisions to wider production losses.
AI might lower search or monitoring costs, but this paper does not study AI. Whether better information changes bargaining or link survival is a follow-up question.
Kopytov's efficient choice of safer techniques is a different mechanism; Elliott studies reliability thresholds in deep networks.
Why is fragility inefficient here?
A buyer and supplier do not capture the full benefit their link creates elsewhere. The distinction is between choosing the network and operating on a given network; I should not say every production-network model is inefficient.
Analytical mechanism under specified complementarities; no causal estimate of AI, tariffs or supplier-support contracts.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
My short version
The useful point for me is that a supply relationship is more than a spot purchase. It takes investment to make an input work for a particular customer, and the relationship creates extra productivity. A shock can make one of these relationships no longer privately worthwhile. When it disappears, other relationships become less attractive too. This can produce a cascade and a sudden output drop even from a small initial change. The sharp result is that this fragility need not be technologically unavoidable: the efficient allocation is continuous in the same shocks. The decentralized incentives to keep links alive are part of the problem (PDF pp. 2–5, 18–25).

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
How the paper gets there
The authors combine a firm-level production network, fixed relationship costs and pairwise Nash bargaining. Two-part tariffs separate marginal input prices from surplus transfers. With a fixed network the equilibrium is efficient; once firms choose links, the network can be too small because a pair does not capture all the benefits it creates elsewhere. I need to keep the uniqueness claims straight: the fixed-network equilibrium is generically unique, while the endogenous network can have multiple equilibria and a greatest equilibrium under the stated complementarity assumptions.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
An OM version could ask which supplier-support contract keeps a critical relationship alive when a temporary cost shock hits. The decision would be a retention payment, minimum purchase commitment or shared investment, rather than a general recommendation to reshore. I would start with a buyer and two upstream tiers, then compare private profit with network-wide lost production. Qualification time and substitutability would matter a lot.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
This is a mechanism paper, not an estimate of the effect of current tariffs. Relationships are selected after shocks in the baseline, so it is not already a model of ex ante safety stock or backup qualification. The supermodularity assumptions limit strong substitution. Adding uncertainty or contracts is an extension the authors themselves mention, so that alone is not a new contribution.

title: The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
text:
Questions for Yannis
Can I formulate a small supplier-retention problem that has a managerial decision and still preserves the externality? What observable evidence would distinguish inefficient link dissolution from an efficient switch to a better supplier?

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
My short version
The helpful idea is that a simple operating standard can change an entire production system. Containers made loading faster and delivery more predictable, which enabled firms to coordinate longer supply chains and leaner inventories. The benefit was not just a cheaper ocean freight rate. That makes this a useful reminder to look for a specific coordination friction instead of assuming that a high-impact OM idea must involve a complicated new algorithm.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
How the paper gets there
The article reports an academic study of container adoption and bilateral trade, including pre-adoption checks. It is journalism discussing another study; the article itself does not provide enough detail for me to evaluate that study's identification. I would read the underlying Bernhofen–El-Sahli–Kneller paper before citing the reported magnitudes as evidence (PDF pp. 1–2).

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
A present-day analogue might be input standards, interoperable supplier documentation or reusable qualification records. The decision is whether several buyers should coordinate on a standard despite implementation costs. An interesting trade-off is that standardization can make switching easier while also encouraging everyone to depend on the same infrastructure.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
I should not repeat the headline that containers matter more than trade agreements as if it were a timeless causal ranking. Historical adoption, infrastructure and policy changed together. This is useful motivation; it does not establish that any modern platform or technology will have a comparable effect.

title: The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
text:
Questions for Yannis
Is there a concrete modern coordination bottleneck in an industry we can access? Would the research be about adoption incentives, the value of reduced lead-time uncertainty, or concentration created by a shared standard?

Can an order or staffing quantity be learned directly using relevant features?

The feature-based newsvendor chooses actions using asymmetric shortage and excess costs. Quantile-regression/ERM and kernel-weighted rules connect statistical learning to the operational loss.

The learning-to-decide idea predates ChatGPT. Generative AI does not invent this connection, although it may change features, interfaces and deployment.

Do supply links transmit a geographically localized disaster?
The earthquake setting makes indirect economic exposure visible. Both suppliers and customers outside the disaster zone can suffer through the network. Geographic distance is not enough to define an unaffected firm.
The next managerial question is which pre-event stock, backup or input-standardization choices help recovery.
AI extraction might extend network measurement; validation and missing-link bias remain separate from identification of propagation.
Inoue–Todo simulates propagation on a large network; this paper estimates effects around an actual shock. Guan simulates lockdown scenarios.

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
text:
My short version
A more accurate prediction need not lead to a better decision. If a small error changes which supplier or route I choose, it can matter much more than a large error that leaves the choice unchanged. SPO measures the cost of the induced decision rather than ordinary prediction error. The practical appeal is that the final workflow can still be predict, then optimize; the training objective is what changes (PDF pp. 1–5, 14).

title: Smart Predict, then Optimize
text:
How the paper gets there
The framework predicts coefficients in a linear objective over a known feasible set. Because the true SPO loss is difficult and potentially discontinuous, the authors derive the convex SPO+ surrogate and give consistency results under distributional conditions. Shortest-path and portfolio experiments compare it with least squares, absolute loss and random forests. The reported advantages are strongest under model misspecification; it is not a theorem that SPO+ beats all predictors in all settings (PDF pp. 26–31).

section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For supply-chain research, I would use this to evaluate whether extra network information changes a sourcing or inventory action. Predicting an upstream link more accurately is only useful if the decision improves. A project could compare an audited extraction pipeline, a simple exposure score and decision-focused learning under missing tier-2 links. The outcome should be cost, fill rate and tail shortage, not just link-prediction accuracy.

text:
What I still need to be careful about
A hidden network can change the feasible set or disruption constraints, whereas the basic framework focuses on unknown objective coefficients with known constraints. I cannot treat the original SPO guarantees as solving uncertain feasibility, rare correlated failures or distribution shift. The paper already suggests constraints and nonlinear objectives as future directions; later work must be checked.

My short version
My main takeaway is that changing the country on an import shipment does not necessarily remove the original upstream dependence. The paper documents a shift in direct U.S. imports away from China toward places such as Vietnam and Mexico, without concluding that global trade is simply disappearing. text:
My short version
The main obstacle is not only optimizing a supply network; it is knowing enough about the network to make a defensible decision. The authors argue for connecting fragmented national firm-level maps into an international map. VAT records, payments and customs data can reveal different parts of the network, but no one source solves the whole problem. Firms often see their own suppliers without seeing several tiers upstream.

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
text:
How the paper gets there
This is a policy/research proposal, not a new estimated intervention effect. It reviews recent microdata developments and sketches a mapping blueprint. Administrative VAT data can give broad domestic coverage; trade data connect across borders. Commercial links often favor large public firms and have limited transparency. Reconstructing missing links is a useful possibility, but a predicted link is not an observed transaction (PDF pp. 2–5).

title: Building an alliance to map global supply networks
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
I would turn the mapping problem into a value-of-information problem. With a small audit budget, which unknown tier-2 relationships should a buyer verify first before choosing suppliers or reserve capacity? The goal would be better decisions with partial information, rather than building a perfect global map. This could pair well with SPO, but the uncertainty in link existence must remain explicit.

text:
What I still need to be careful about
Getting access to VAT or bank records is a major institutional hurdle. A supply link does not reveal quantities, substitutability, inventories or unused capacity. Also, missing links are unlikely to be random. A method that works only when links are hidden uniformly at random might look good in a benchmark and fail on smaller or overseas suppliers.

Ama tedarik ağı değişirken, politika belirsizliği varken, alternatif kaynağın onayı aylar sürerken ve kararları artık insanlar AI ile birlikte verirken, aynı stok kararının anlamı değişebilir. Kabaca, OR bir problemi nasıl modelleyip çözeceğimize; OM işletmenin hangi kararı neden vereceğine ve sonucuna; ekonomi ise teşviklere, piyasa tepkilerine ve refaha odaklanabilir. text:
Altı başlıkta ne oluyor?

1. Üretim ağları ve kesintilerin yayılması
Bir fabrika yalnızca kendi tedarikçisine bağlı değil; onun tedarikçilerine, kritik malzemeye ve müşterilerinin durumuna da bağlı. Network Origins bunun neden ekonominin toplam dalgalanmasına dönüşebildiğini anlatan temel çalışma. Carvalho gerçek Japonya depreminden yayılma kanıtı getiriyor. Guan ve Inoue–Todo farklı ölçeklerde senaryoları simüle ediyor. Simülasyon sonucunu gözlenmiş nedensel etki diye sunmamalıyım.
Daha yeni soru, bu ağı sabit kabul etmemek: firmalar hangi ilişkiyi kuruyor veya bırakıyor? Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi ilişkilerin pazarlık ve teşvikler nedeniyle zincirleme kopabileceğini; Elliott güvenilirlik yatırımı ve eşik davranışını; Kopytov belirsizlikte daha güvenli ama pahalı üretim seçimini inceliyor.
OM bağlantısı: Hangi ilişkiyi koruyayım, hangi noktaya stok veya yedek kapasite koyayım? Ama önce hangi mekanizmanın geçerli olduğunu anlamalıyım.


2. Üretim başka ülkelere kayıyor; bağımlılık gerçekten değişiyor mu?
Alfaro–Chor, ABD’nin doğrudan tedarikinin nasıl değiştiğini gösteriyor. Dhyne, ithalat yapmayan yerli bir firmanın bile yerli tedarikçiler üzerinden yabancı girdilere bağlı olabileceğini anlatıyor. Çin’den alınan ürünün artık Vietnam’dan gelmesi tek başına bütün bağımlılığın bittiğini göstermiyor. Aynı şekilde Çinli sahiplik veya Çin girdisi görmek de otomatik olarak yasa dışı transshipment demek değil.
Geography üretim aşamalarının nerede olacağını, Organizing hangi aşamanın firma bünyesinde olacağını, Elementary Theory hata olasılıklarının aşama dağılımını nasıl etkilediğini açıklayan farklı temeller. Fajgelbaum tarifelerin maliyetini kimin taşıdığına bakıyor.
OM bağlantısı: Yer değişikliği sırasında sipariş, stok, kalite onayı, teslim süresi ve kapasite nasıl yönetiliyor? Sadece “hangi ülke kazandı?” sorusunun ötesine geçmek gerekiyor.


3. Dayanıklılık tek bir ölçü değil
Daha az kesinti yaşamak, kesintide az kaybetmek ve hızlı toparlanmak farklı sonuçlar. Tomlin stok, güvenilir kaynak ve kesinti sonrası tepkiyi ayırıyor. Base–surge ucuz ve yavaş kaynaktan temel akışı, hızlı kaynaktan esnek desteği birleştiriyor; kaynak ve talep değişkenliğini içeriyor, fakat Tomlin’in kesinti modelinin aynısı değil.
Jain 2014 tedariki stok yatırımıyla ilişkilendiriyor. Jain 2022 çeşitlendirmenin daha yavaş, uzun ilişkilerin daha hızlı toparlanmayla ilişkili olduğunu buluyor. Niu 2025 firmaların pandemi döneminde gerçekten hangi tedarikçi, ülke ve sevkiyat değişikliklerini yaptığını inceliyor. Gözlenen bir değişikliğin işe yaradığını söylemek için ayrıca performans ölçmek gerekiyor.
Örnek cevap: “Çeşitlendirme her bakımdan iyi veya kötü değil. Stok maliyetini, riskin birlikte gerçekleşmesini, tedarikçi teşvikini ve toparlanmayı ayrı ölçmeliyim.”


4. Ağı görmek ile doğru karar verebilmek farklı
Science mapping alliance yazısı firmalar arası ağların hangi verilerle haritalanabileceğini soruyor. Lee–So–Tang çok daha eski bir makalede belirli bir talep bilgisinin üretici için değerini modelliyor. Yani “bilgi önemlidir” yeni bir araştırma sonucu değil.
Yeni veri ve AI daha çok ilişki bulmayı sağlayabilir. Fakat firma A’nın firma B ile ilişkisi olması, benim kullandığım parçanın oradan geldiğini veya B’de boş kapasite olduğunu göstermeyebilir. Eksik ilişki de bağımsızlık kanıtı değildir.
OM bağlantısı: Hangi bilgiyi doğrulamak için para harcamalıyım ve öğrendiğim bilgi hangi uygulanabilir kararı değiştiriyor? Önceki ilk fikir bu başlığın bir alt dalı; seçilmiş tez konusu değil.


5. Tahminden karara, sonra üretken AI’a
Ban–Rudin, özelliklerden maliyete uygun sipariş/personel miktarı öğreniyor. Bertsimas–Kallus, bağlama göre karar vermeyi; SPO, tahmin modelini tahmin hatası yerine oluşturduğu kararın maliyetiyle eğitmeyi ele alıyor. Bunlar ChatGPT’den önce gelişmiş bağlantılar.
ORLM doğal dilden optimizasyon modeli ve kod üretmeye çalışıyor. Teknik testlerin yanında 30 katılımcılı sınırlı bir insan yardımı çalışması da var. Bu, bütün işletmelerde verim artışı kanıtı değil. OptiGuide mevcut modelin etrafında “şu kapasiteyi azaltırsak ne olur?” gibi soruları cevaplayan bir arayüz kuruyor. Çözücü hâlâ önemli; yanlış kurulan bir problemi çok iyi çözmek doğru iş kararını garantilemiyor.
Dai–Swaminathan üç alan ayırıyor: AI’ın operasyonlarda kullanılması, AI sistemlerinin geliştirme/işletme süreçlerinin OM ile tasarlanması ve insan–AI etkileşimi. Bu nedenle “AI neyi değiştirdi?” sorusunu yalnızca tahmin doğruluğuyla cevaplamak dar kalır.


6. Tarih ve büyük resim
Outside the Box, seçilen bölümlerde küreselleşmenin organizasyonunu; Humble Hero konteynerleri ve koordinasyon değişimini anlamaya yardım ediyor. The Box tam metni bu turda okunamadı. 2019 Economist raporunun da tam metnine erişilemedi; o kaydı ayrıntılı okunmuş gibi anlatmamalıyım.
Tarihsel bağlantı şu: bazen büyük değişim yeni bir algoritmadan değil, standardizasyon ve tamamlayıcı altyapıdan geliyor. Ama konteynerlerden hareketle “AI da aynı etkiyi yapacak” sonucu çıkaramayız.

title: Yannis görüşmesi: Türkçe hazırlık
section: AI sonrasında gerçekten ne değişmiş olabilir?
text:
AI sonrasında gerçekten ne değişmiş olabilir?
Üç şeyi ayrı tutmak istiyorum:

Araç değişiyor: Tahmin, veri çıkarma ve model kurma ucuzlayabilir veya hızlanabilir. Bunun kararı iyileştirip iyileştirmediğini ölçmeliyim.
Organizasyon değişiyor: Kim öneriyor, kim kontrol ediyor, kim istisna kararı veriyor? AI rutin işleri hızlandırsa bile insanın inceleme kapasitesi darboğaz olabilir. Bu bir araştırma mekanizması; listedeki her makalenin kanıtladığı sonuç değil.
AI’ın kendisi talep yaratıyor: Çip, sunucu, veri merkezi, elektrik ve soğutmanın birlikte hazır olması gerekiyor. Birinde kapasite varken diğerinin eksik olması yatırımı bekletebilir. Burada kapasite, sözleşme, yer seçimi ve koordinasyon soruları var.

2026 MSOM vision yazısı bu genişlemeyi güncel bir gündem olarak ele alıyor. IEA’nın 2026 özeti de veri merkezi talebi ile çip/enerji ekipmanı darboğazlarını tartışıyor. Bu yüzden AI, yalnızca tedarik zincirini optimize eden araç değil, tedarik zincirine ihtiyaç duyan bir faaliyet alanı da olabilir. Bununla birlikte bu liste AI’ın bütün sektörlerde dayanıklılığı artırdığını nedensel olarak göstermiyor.

title: Yannis görüşmesi: Türkçe hazırlık
text:
Yannis sorarsa kısa yanıtlar







Sorabileceği soru
Benim verebileceğim cevap




“Ee, OM dünyasında neler oluyormuş?”
“Bu seçkide ağların ve tedarik coğrafyasının nasıl değiştiği, firmaların hangi operasyonel tepkiyi verdiği ve bunun maliyet/toparlanma sonuçları öne çıkıyor. AI tarafında da karar yöntemleri kadar iş akışı ve AI’ın kendi kapasite ihtiyacı var.”


“Bunlar zaten bilinen şeyler değil mi?”
“Temel kararların çoğu eski. Yenilik iddiasını ortamın veya verinin yeni olmasına dayandıramam; yeni koşulun önemli bir mekanizma ya da farklı karar yarattığını göstermem gerekir.”


“Hangi makale senin için başlangıç olur?”
“Operasyonel değişiklikleri görmek için Niu; ekonomide mekanizmaları ayırmak için Kopytov ile Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi; AI alanını düzenlemek için Dai–Swaminathan.”


“En şaşırtıcı bulgu?”
“Çeşitlendirmenin her performans boyutunda üstün olmaması. Jain’in toparlanma sonucu, daha çok tedarikçi sayısını tek başına dayanıklılık diye kullanmamam gerektiğini düşündürdü.”


“Daha güvenli ağ neden her zaman daha iyi değil?”
“Güvenliğin üretkenlik ve maliyet bedeli olabilir. Kopytov’da daha düşük çıktı, riskten kaçınma nedeniyle verimli bir tercihle uyumlu.”


“Niu bize neyi kanıtlamıyor?”
“Sevkiyat ve tedarik portföyü değişimini gözlüyor; tam stok hedeflerini, alt kademe değişimini veya her tepkinin nedensel başarısını göstermiyor.”


“AI burada nerede?”
“Önce hangi rol olduğunu belirlemeliyim: tahmin/karar yöntemi mi, planlayıcı arayüzü mü, iş bölümü değişikliği mi, yoksa çip–enerji kapasite problemi mi?”


“SPO ile ORLM farkı ne?”
“SPO tahminin eğitim hedefini karar maliyetine bağlıyor. ORLM problem tanımından model/kod üretiyor. Birinin başarı ölçüsü diğerinin sorusunu cevaplamıyor.”


“Neden OM, neden sadece ekonomi değil?”
“Bir yöneticinin uygulanabilir kararını ve servis, maliyet, stok veya toparlanma sonucunu incelemek istiyorum. Ekonomi ise teşvikleri ve piyasa/çevre etkilerini doğru kurmama yardım ediyor.”


“Veri nereden gelecek?”
“Henüz erişimi doğrulamadık. Ticaret verisi bazı betimlemeleri mümkün kılar; ürün onayı, gerçek boş kapasite ve karar kayıtları için kurum ya da firma erişimi gerekebilir.”


“Ne araştırmak istiyorsun?”
“Şu an seçmekten önce üç bağlantıyı karşılaştırıyorum: politika belirsizliğinde operasyonel uyum, bilgi ile eylem arasındaki koordinasyon ve AI’ın iş akışı/kapasite etkisi. Hangisine daha derin gireceğimi sizinle tartışmak istiyorum.”


“Nature/Science okuyunca katkı OM olur mu?”
“Konuya neden önem vermem gerektiğini oradan öğrenebilirim. OM katkısı için ayrıca karar, mekanizma, sağlam karşılaştırma ve performans kanıtı gerekir.”

title: Supply chains: an OM–economics field map
section: My answer to “what is happening in OM?”
text:
My answer to “what is happening in OM?”
My reading of this selection is that the interesting questions connect operating choices, changing production networks and wider economic consequences. The underlying decisions—inventory, sourcing, information sharing and capacity—are established OM questions. What changes is the environment, what can be observed, and which consequences a study needs to explain.
I would distinguish three developments. First, firms adapt their supplier relationships and production locations in response to uncertainty and policy, so the network cannot always be held fixed. Second, researchers can sometimes connect transactions, shipping and accounting data to observe those adjustments, although access and measurement remain major constraints. Third, AI changes the cost of prediction, formulation and interaction, while creating new workflow and physical-infrastructure problems. These developments create questions at the OM–economics boundary; they do not make all older inventory or sourcing research obsolete.
This is a synthesis of a deliberately selected reading list and a small current-literature check, not a bibliometric ranking of the whole field. This list is strong on production networks, trade, sourcing and decision methods. It is thin on labor, contracts in AI supply chains, climate adaptation, circularity, humanitarian operations, transport and causal evaluations of actual AI adoption. Those are omissions to address before selecting a topic, not evidence that they are unimportant.

title: Supply chains: an OM–economics field map
text:
A six-part field map










Area
Economic question
OM question
Main anchors in the original 38
What feels current; what is established




A. Production networks and systemic resilience
How do local shocks affect aggregate production, and do private incentives create excessive fragility?
Which relationships, buffers or recovery capabilities should be protected?
Network Origins; Beyond Hulten; Carvalho; Elliott; Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi; Kopytov; QJE resilience; Guan; Inoue; Baldwin–Freeman
Propagation is established. Endogenous networks, adaptation and private–social comparisons develop the question further.


B. Trade, geography and organization
Who produces which stage, who owns it, and who bears trade-policy costs?
How should buyers qualify sources, allocate orders and manage transition costs?
Alfaro–Chor; Dhyne; Fajgelbaum; JPE resilience; Geography; Organizing; Elementary Theory; NAFTA; Chinese firms; McKinsey
Geography and ownership are older foundations. Current reallocation and policy uncertainty create settings in which to test adjustment and operating consequences.


C. Sourcing, inventory and recovery
How do coordination and relationship incentives shape adjustment?
When do stocks, responsive capacity, long relationships and diversification help different outcomes?
Tomlin; Jain 2014; Jain 2022; Niu 2025; base–surge; HBR
The trade-offs predate COVID and generative AI. Measuring which response works, for whom and under which constraints is the continuing task.


D. Information, visibility and coordination
Who produces or shares information, and who captures its benefits?
Which signal changes a feasible action enough to justify acquiring and validating it?
Science mapping alliance; Lee–So–Tang; links to Dhyne and SPO
Information value is established. New data and extraction tools broaden possibilities but bring selective coverage and validation problems.


E. Data-to-decision and AI-enabled operations
How do technology, incentives and organizational design change decisions and adoption?
How should learning, optimization, human review and execution fit together?
Ban–Rudin; Bertsimas–Kallus; SPO; ORLM; OptiGuide; Dai–Swaminathan
Decision-aware learning precedes LLMs. Generative interfaces and formulation are newer; end-to-end operating impact requires separate evidence.


F. Historical change and broad motivation
How do coordination technologies and institutions reshape globalization?
Which complementary standards, capabilities and infrastructures make a system work?
Outside the Box; The Box; Humble Hero; Economist 2019
Useful chronology and cases. Historical analogy and journalism motivate questions but do not establish causality or novelty.



Papers can belong to several areas. Each item is assigned one primary area below for navigation, not to imply separate disciplines or mutually exclusive methods. IE, OR, OM and economics overlap. The distinction I need is the question and contribution: a faster algorithm, an operating policy, an empirically established mechanism or an equilibrium/welfare result.

title: Supply chains: an OM–economics field map
section: The connections I should be able to explain
text:
The connections I should be able to explain

1. From propagation to network choice
Network Origins explains why asymmetric input links can make local shocks aggregate. Carvalho supplies empirical evidence of transmission after an actual earthquake. Beyond Hulten shows why nonlinearities and substitution matter beyond first-order accounting. Inoue and Guan provide simulation-based approaches with different units and assumptions.
The newer mechanism papers then ask why firms choose the links and reliability they do. Elliott studies reliability thresholds and investment; Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi studies relationship gains, bargaining and link dissolution; Kopytov studies ex ante technique choice under uncertainty. These are complementary explanations, not three estimates of the same effect. Kopytov’s efficient flight to safety is a useful counterexample to the idea that every output loss indicates excessive private fragility.
OM bridge: observe a specific operating choice—supplier retention, stock, qualification or capacity—and ask whether it changes the transmission or recovery mechanism. A network centrality score by itself is not a policy, and adding a familiar decision to a large network is not automatically a new contribution.


2. From direct trade flows to operational adjustment
Alfaro–Chor documents changing direct sourcing. Dhyne shows how domestic links transmit foreign exposure. Antràs–de Gortari explains stage-level geography; Antràs–Chor explains ownership; Costinot–Vogel–Wang isolates reliability in sequential specialization. These distinguish where, who controls, and what input is needed.
Niu makes the OM bridge more tangible by observing supplier, country and shipment adjustments. Jain connects sourcing with working capital and recovery. Fajgelbaum and Caliendo–Parro connect policy costs to economic incidence and welfare. I would not use any one of these to assert that reshoring universally increases resilience.
OM bridge: study the adjustment path and its consequences—qualified capacity, delivery performance, inventories and total cost—rather than simply count announcements or countries.


3. Why resilience findings can appear to disagree
“Resilience” may mean fewer interruptions, less lost production during an interruption, faster recovery, lower financial volatility or higher expected welfare. Those outcomes can move differently. Diversification may reduce an exposure and still weaken volume incentives or make recovery coordination harder. Inventory can absorb a short interruption but not a long one. A nearby source helps only if its relevant capability is available.
The Jain recovery evidence is an association based on an inferred recovery measure, not a general causal law against diversification. The JPE and QJE models identify conditional incentive differences; they do not say any particular firm has chosen badly. I need to name the outcome and benchmark before using “more resilient.”


4. From more information to better action
Lee–So–Tang establishes information value in a specified two-level demand setting. The Science alliance article concerns network measurement and institutional access. The related 2023 Culot methodological critique, already in the follow-up library, cautions that corporate supplier relationships need not be the relevant product flows. These are different information objects.
SPO, Ban–Rudin and Bertsimas–Kallus explain how prediction and data should be assessed through operational loss. None establishes that an inferred supplier edge is a verified alternative or that unknown constraints are covered by a known-feasible-set learning framework.
A correction worth remembering: the original Lee–So–Tang discussion should not be reduced to “higher autocorrelation always makes sharing more valuable.” Babai et al. (2016), accepted manuscript/abstract qualifies that monotonic claim. I checked this at abstract level; I have not audited the correction’s derivation.

title: Supply chains: an OM–economics field map
section: What AI changes—and what these papers actually establish
text:
What AI changes—and what these papers actually establish









Layer
What changes
Evidence in this list
What I can responsibly say




Prediction and contextual decisions
Rich features can inform cost-sensitive decisions
Ban–Rudin; Bertsimas–Kallus; SPO
Established before the recent LLM wave. Better average forecast accuracy is not sufficient evidence of better operating decisions.


Formulation
Natural language can be converted into a model and solver code
ORLM
Technical benchmarks and a limited human-assistance study support potential in specified tasks. Correct code execution does not prove the intended problem was correctly modeled.


Interaction
Planners can ask what-if questions and obtain explanations around a solver
OptiGuide
Demonstrates a workflow and a Microsoft application. It does not establish a causal improvement in resilience or calibrated managerial trust.


Workflow, responsibility and adoption
Humans need review, exception handling and clear decision rights
Dai–Swaminathan
Current OM framework highlights these questions. Its synthesis is not one new causal experiment.


AI’s own operations and physical supply chain
Deployment needs data pipelines and monitoring; AI scale also needs chips, servers, power and cooling
Dai–Swaminathan plus current MSOM/IEA sources
Distinguish operating AI systems from supplying their physical infrastructure. Both offer OM questions. Physical capacity remains scarce even when prediction becomes cheaper.



My strongest distinction is AI as a method versus AI as a change in the phenomenon. A new forecasting model can be a method for an old inventory problem. A firm delegating procurement decisions changes workflows and incentives. A surge in compute demand creates a capacity and investment-coordination setting. These require different evidence and may lead to different contributions.
Possible AI mechanisms to investigate include cheaper search and verification, faster formulation, changed human attention, common model errors, and coupled chip/power investments. These are research possibilities, not results inferred from the 38 papers. In particular, shared AI use causing synchronized shortages or a new bullwhip effect needs direct prior-work search and evidence before it can be called a gap.

title: Supply chains: an OM–economics field map
section: A dated update beyond the original list
text:
A dated update beyond the original list
These sources update the picture as of 20 October 2026. They are supplementary context, not additional members of the original 38.

Alfaro–Chor, NBER 34490, November 2025, revised April 2026. The abstract reports continued US sourcing reallocation, concentrated among major partners, with adjustment spreading to relationship-sticky goods. It distinguishes China decoupling from withdrawal from world trade. This is a separate paper from the 2023 reading, not an update silently substituted for it. Primary record. Coverage: abstract/record only.
Cohen et al., MSOM, published online 26 March 2026. A community vision organizes AI and supply chains around intelligence, execution, strategy, people and infrastructure. I take its integration and physical-supply-chain agenda as a signal of current OM questions, not as measured adoption impact or proof of consensus across all OM research. Selected abstract, introduction and infrastructure sections consulted. Primary article.
IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI, 2026. Its updated executive summary projects data-centre electricity consumption around 950 TWh in 2030, roughly 3% of global electricity demand, with near-term equipment and chip constraints. These are projections for data centres, not electricity already consumed by AI alone. I use this primary sector outlook to motivate capacity coordination and avoid repeating an unverified much higher percentage from a commentary. Executive summary. Coverage: executive summary only.

The follow-up collection also contains Nature/Nature Communications, network-information and measurement sources from the earlier targeted review. They can enrich several branches of this map; their presence does not mean the upstream-risk branch has been selected.

How the broad-interest outlets change my reading
I read Econometrica, QJE, JPE and REStud for mechanisms, identification and welfare arguments. Science’s Policy Forum motivates a broad measurement institution; Nature Human Behaviour and Nature Sustainability supply modeling settings and societal outcomes; they are distinct journals from flagship Nature. The Economist and HBR help find concrete puzzles and explain why a reader should care, but are not equivalent to academic causal evidence. Books provide historical mechanisms and chronology.
For an OM contribution I still need a meaningful operating choice and a result that changes how that choice is understood. A topical setting or a broad-interest citation cannot substitute for that contribution. A buyer-level study need not estimate general equilibrium; a policy/welfare recommendation needs more than showing that a buyer’s cost falls. These are evidence standards I am learning from the papers, not predictions about where a future paper will be accepted.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
My revised assessment
The starting question is important, but the basic mechanism is already established. Different direct suppliers can share an upstream source; this can change optimal mitigation and transmit financial risk. Neither this observation, adding inventory to it, nor asking whether information has value is sufficient novelty.
My more defensible question to investigate is:

When does verifying a hidden common upstream dependency create usable diversification, once a buyer must qualify and activate an alternative before its inventory buffer is exhausted?

“Usable” is a working description, not a new construct that I can claim to have invented. I mean a product-specific alternative with verified relevant upstream exposure, acceptable quality, available capacity and a feasible activation date. A firm name, different country or predicted link alone does not establish that.
The potential contribution would be a new, well-measured operational fact and a decision mechanism, supported by a convincing comparison with existing models. Its novelty is still conditional. Full-text comparison with the closest information papers is unfinished because several manuscripts could not be accessed.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
The closest obstacles to novelty
Ang et al. is the first benchmark. Its model already makes a common tier-2 source affect the buyer’s mitigation strategy and suppliers’ incentives. The precise baseline information assumption appears on printed p. 2401 (PDF p. 6). I cannot describe the basic diamond structure or a stock/sourcing comparison as my contribution.
The information question is also crowded. Bakshi–Mohan and its 2025 companion directly challenge the idea that “we add an audit” is enough. The latter’s abstract even reports a non-obvious comparative static for perfect-information value. I must obtain both full texts before making a theorem-level novelty claim.
Measurement and action are established concerns too. Culot warns about interpreting corporate relationships as relevant product flows, Mungo discusses substantive evaluation, and the September 2026 JBL paper addresses conversion of visibility into action. The remaining opportunity needs a specific decision, observable constraint and result beyond those general messages.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: The candidate contribution I would test first
text:
The candidate contribution I would test first
A working title is “From supplier diversification to a ready alternative: the operating value of verifying shared upstream dependence.” This is a project description, not a submission-ready title.
I would narrow to one input family and one critical process stage. The initial decision maker is one buyer. Before a disruption, it can spend a limited budget on verifying a suspected common dependency, qualifying an independently exposed alternative, or holding a buffer. Qualification takes time; a claimed alternate supplier may lack the required grade, process approval or reserved capacity.
The proposed mechanism is that information and readiness can be complements. Learning the correct bottleneck may be valuable only when it changes a feasible action in time. Conversely, qualification can be wasted if the nominal alternative relies on the same constrained source. These are hypotheses to test against the literature, not results established by this review.
A small example helps state the distinction. If inventory covers 20 days but a genuinely independent alternative needs 60 days for approval, discovering that alternative during the disruption does not protect the first uncovered weeks. An already qualified source may help, but only if it has accessible capacity and does not share the affected bottleneck. These numbers are hypothetical. This example is not a novel theorem; recovery/coverage logic has substantial prior work.
What would make the project more than an incremental model? At least one of the following, with evidence:

A documented decision reversal: the same budget produces a different preferred action once product/site dependence and qualification feasibility replace a supplier-name count. Show when an established, correctly implemented baseline would not already recommend that action.
A credible estimate of the benefit of information conditional on operational readiness, using observed procurement and service outcomes rather than risk perceptions alone.
A quantitatively important, validated mismeasurement result: nominal diversification systematically misstates relevant independence in the selected setting, and correcting it materially changes a real decision. This needs more than showing that some database links are wrong.

I would begin with the second route if we have a partner and decision logs. Otherwise, I would start with a small model and an openly reproducible sector pilot, while being explicit that the pilot does not establish firm-level performance or publication-level novelty.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: Evidence and data I would need
text:
Evidence and data I would need
The useful unit is buyer–part or material grade–production site–date, not just buyer–supplier firm. Minimum fields are:

Direct source and the specific common upstream process/site, with evidence and verification date.
Whether an alternative is technically qualified for the same requirement; qualification start/end dates and any approval restrictions.
Available or reserved capacity, lead time, inventory coverage and the actual contingency chosen.
Disruption timing and operating outcomes: unfilled units, delivery delay, downtime, expediting cost and recovery.

Keep four distinctions separate: unobserved is not independent; common ownership is not necessarily a common physical bottleneck; a shared node is not necessarily relevant to the focal product; and a technically feasible alternative is not necessarily available under widespread stress.
A sample of 10–30 verified part/site cases could expose measurement and access problems before a larger project. That would be a feasibility exercise, not a sufficient sample for a general causal conclusion. A suitable power calculation and dependence structure would be needed for an evaluation design.

A feasible public-data starting point
Cheng et al. provide public code and data and an archived release. The repository has processed flows, raw trade files and analysis scripts. It offers a concrete way to reproduce stage-level dependence and uncertainty bounds. The material is historical and aggregated by country, and some inputs are embedded in scripts. I have verified availability, not run a replication.
The June 2025 correction changes two labels in Fig. 4e and adds a rounding note; it is attached with the corrected paper. A pilot must use the corrected version. Public flows cannot substitute for product qualification or actual reserved-capacity data.
Panjiva or FactSet could provide signals and a sampling frame if our institution has access. Neither should be treated as a complete bill of materials. A missing edge is not proof that two alternatives are independent. The Brazilian transactions used by Monteiro et al. are proprietary; their existence is not evidence that our group can obtain them.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: How to distinguish an OM contribution from an algorithm project
text:
How to distinguish an OM contribution from an algorithm project
The central outcome is an operating decision and its consequences: which verification, buffer or qualification investment should a buyer make, and what service or cost improves? A new optimizer, larger graph or more accurate link classifier would be a tool, not the core claim.
A first model could hold demand and other buyers’ behavior simple and compare:

The buyer’s current rule and a nominal supplier-count rule.
Known correlated risk with a correctly implemented Ang-style incentive/sourcing benchmark.
A Ford-style exposure/contingency baseline once its full model is reviewed.
Fixed versus targeted verification; qualification-only and buffer-only policies.
A full-information benchmark with the same physical capacity and timing constraints.

Do not handicap the baselines by pretending that the literature assumes independent suppliers when it does not. Report total cost, service, severe shortfall and realized recovery, including verification and qualification costs. Evaluate map errors that disproportionately hide critical links, not only random deletion.
If budget accounting treats audit spending and inventory spending as substitutes, that is a modeling choice to justify, not an empirical fact. The first result should remain visible in a small example; complexity can come later.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: A credible empirical route, if data exist
text:
A credible empirical route, if data exist
A partner’s phased introduction of verified upstream information could provide a setting, but voluntary adoption is endogenous: better firms may map more, and disrupted firms may map after a problem. Information-arrival timestamps are also often influenced by anticipated risk.
A field design could compare normal planning, verified dependency information, and information plus a defined prequalification support process. Randomization would need to respect shared suppliers and spillovers; withholding already-known safety-critical information would not be an appropriate design. The implementation and sample requirements would have to be agreed with a partner. There is no experiment in place.
Without randomization, a phased rollout or other external variation might support identification only after examining assignment, anticipation, pretrends, demand shifts and concurrent changes. A simple event study does not solve those problems. A descriptive paper should label its estimates as descriptive.
The high-value outcome would connect what was learned → what action became feasible → what was actually changed → what operating consequence followed. Interview explanations can guide the mechanism but cannot replace performance evidence.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
text:
Why the broader journals matter
I would borrow the question selection and breadth of these outlets, not assume that a small sourcing model fits all of them.

Science: Pichler et al. (2023), already in the library, motivates network visibility as a broad data and coordination problem. Our narrower contribution must identify the buyer action enabled by better information.
Nature Communications: Cheng et al. gives a concrete, societally important battery setting. It is not the flagship Nature. A strong sector study would need physical/process knowledge and defensible data, not only a general supplier graph.
Nature: Guan’s October 2026 piece is a Comment. It motivates common infrastructure dependencies but is not causal evidence. Digital/energy dependencies are a later application unless we can observe and act on one of them clearly.
Econometrica: Kopytov et al. (2024), already in the library, reminds me that safer sourcing and efficient resource allocation are different questions. Lower volatility is not automatically welfare improvement.
QJE: Grossman–Helpman–Sabal distinguishes private protective investment from network-wide incentives. A subsidy or public information-sharing proposal would require an explicit externality, not just a buyer saving money.
The Economist: Useful for finding contemporary cases and explaining why someone should care. It does not establish a literature gap or identify a causal effect. I did not add a tangential or inaccessible article merely to include the outlet.

A buyer-level operating result could naturally be assessed in OM outlets such as Management Science, MSOM, POM or JOM, depending on method and evidence. A claim about society-wide resilience would need broader validation. No venue or acceptance probability is implied by this review.

title: Candidate 1: shared upstream risk
section: What I would say to Yannis
text:
What I would say to Yannis

“The closer search changed my view. The common tier-2 problem is already modeled by Ang and coauthors and studied empirically by Wang and coauthors. There are also direct papers on network information and its value. So I would not pitch hidden dependence itself as new. I would like to investigate when learning a product-specific dependency changes a feasible mitigation action, especially when qualifying an independent alternative takes longer than the inventory buffer. I think the first task is to establish whether we can observe that decision and whether it remains distinct from those benchmarks.”


Questions he may ask







Question
My answer at this stage




“What exactly is new?”
Not yet established. The candidate margin is verified information interacting with readiness for a specific product and bottleneck, with operating outcomes. I must compare the closest full texts first.


“Isn’t this Ang plus an information cost?”
It would be too incremental if that is all it becomes. I need a mechanism or empirical decision effect not already implied by its known-configuration model and existing information-value work.


“Isn’t this just time-to-recover versus inventory coverage?”
Timing itself is established. The proposed test is how product-specific learning changes which independent response can be qualified in time, evaluated against exposure/contingency baselines.


“Why not map everything?”
Full mapping is costly and may not change feasible actions; that general insight already has prior work. We would need to show a specific allocation of verification and readiness effort that changes an important decision.


“Where is the data?”
Open battery flows permit a limited pilot. The actual buyer question requires product/site, qualification, capacity and outcome data; we have not confirmed access.


“What if independence cannot be observed?”
Then we cannot certify it from missing commercial links. We should narrow to a validated subnetwork or change the question.


“Is this general interest?”
The broad problem is whether costly de-risking buys continuity. The contribution would need a compelling fact and a clear operating mechanism. Journal labels cannot supply either.


“Why not model all firms and policy?”
That would add a second project. First establish the buyer decision; only then ask whether its incentives differ from network welfare.

section: First milestones and reasons to stop
text:
First milestones and reasons to stop

Read Ang’s model alongside the full Wang article, Bakshi–Mohan, Bakshi’s companion, the latest Osadchiy manuscript and the Ford implementation. The inaccessible texts are a genuine remaining comparison task.
Write a one-page assumption comparison: known versus uncertain topology; static versus changing links; perfect versus noisy signals; stock position; qualification; actual capacity; decentralized incentives; operating versus financial outcomes. Do not infer absent assumptions from abstracts.
Check whether a firm partner or an existing institutional dataset can supply the minimum fields. Select one input family only after this check.
Reproduce a public-data baseline and a small decision example. Predefine what would count as a meaningful action change.
Stop or pivot if a closest paper already solves the same choice, independence cannot be validated, the decision improvement disappears against a fair baseline, or feasible data cannot measure the operating outcome.

title: Meeting with Yannis: understanding the field
text:
My opening answer
“I initially thought supply chains were mainly an established set of inventory and logistics problems. What I am seeing in this list is a connection between operating choices and wider economic questions: how networks form and adjust, how shocks spread, when private resilience differs from social resilience, and what new data can actually tell us. AI adds both decision tools and new organizational and infrastructure questions. I have not chosen a topic yet; I want to understand which of these connections is both important and feasible to study.”

Five comparisons I want to get right







Comparison
What I need to distinguish




Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi vs Kopytov

Alfaro–Chor / Dhyne / Niu

Jain inventory vs Jain recovery

title: Meeting with Yannis: understanding the field
text:
Read closely: 19 discussion cards
Each card connects to the fuller source note, which contains the existing mechanism, method and source-version detail. I should explain the mechanism before repeating any number. In particular, the local JPE, Carvalho, Dhyne, Jain and other manuscripts are not all the final published versions.

1. The Macroeconomics of Supply Chain Disruptions
Question: Why can a small shock destroy productive supply relationships?
My takeaway: I see the key change as treating the network itself as a choice. Relationship-specific gains and bargaining can make privately chosen links disappear in a cascade, even when an efficient allocation would adjust continuously.
If Yannis asks “Why is fragility inefficient here?”
A buyer and supplier do not capture the full benefit their link creates elsewhere. The distinction is between choosing the network and operating on a given network; I should not say every production-network model is inefficient.
Connection: Kopytov’s efficient choice of safer techniques is a different mechanism; Elliott studies reliability thresholds in deep networks.
Boundary: Analytical mechanism under specified complementarities; no causal estimate of AI, tariffs or supplier-support contracts.
Open detailed source note.


2. Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
Question: How do firms rewire their input choices when uncertainty increases?
My takeaway: Safer sourcing can reduce volatility while sacrificing productivity. In this model the equilibrium trade-off can be efficient. I need to compare welfare, expected output and volatility separately.
If Yannis asks “Does lower GDP mean firms chose badly?”
Not necessarily. A risk-averse household values stability. Lower expected GDP and lower welfare are different claims. The welfare benchmark matters before proposing a subsidy.
Connection: Acemoglu–Tahbaz-Salehi emphasizes a network externality; this paper shows that a move toward safety need not itself be a market failure.
Boundary: The sectoral calibration and financial risk proxies do not directly measure a buyer’s delivery risk or qualification time.
Open detailed source note.


3. Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
Question: Should policy encourage diversification or domestic sourcing?
My takeaway: There are competing private incentives: keeping products available helps consumers, while surviving when rivals fail can attract their demand. This is why I cannot start from the claim that firms always underinvest in resilience.
If Yannis asks “So should governments subsidize reshoring?”
The consulted working paper gives conditional results. Under CES demand and restricted instruments diversification can be the constrained-optimal intervention; broader demand assumptions can change its direction. I would not recommend universal reshoring.
Connection: Tomlin asks what one buyer should do; this paper asks whether private choices line up with social welfare.
Boundary: The local source is the June 2022 working paper, not a line-by-line check of the 2023 published version.
Open detailed source note.


4. Global Supply Chains: The Looming Great Reallocation
Question: Is US sourcing disappearing or changing its geography?
My takeaway: The useful distinction is direct import origin versus the upstream production ecosystem. A fall in direct imports from China does not by itself measure a fall in Chinese inputs or ownership elsewhere.
If Yannis asks “Is this evidence of deglobalization?”
It documents reallocation of direct sourcing and several related indicators. I would separate decoupling from China from a general retreat from trade, then ask whether indirect exposure also changed.
Connection: Niu looks at firm–product sourcing actions; Dhyne exposes indirect foreign dependence. The newer Alfaro–Chor paper is a separate 2025/2026 follow-up.
Boundary: Descriptive patterns are not a causal test of whether a particular buyer’s nearshoring improved service.
Open detailed source note.


5. Supply Network Formation and Fragility
Question: Why can a network withstand isolated failures but remain systemically fragile?
My takeaway: Alternative suppliers within one input category help, but a producer still needs every essential category. In a sufficiently deep network, reliability can change sharply near a threshold, and private investment can leave the network near it.
If Yannis asks “Does this predict an imminent real-world collapse?”
No. It establishes a threshold mechanism in a large/deep-network model. Applying it requires finite-network data and a check of its essential-input and failure assumptions.
Connection: Network Origins has amplification on a given input–output network; this paper adds reliability and strategic relationship investment.
Boundary: No measured distance of today’s economy from a collapse threshold, and no evidence that AI solves it.
Open detailed source note.


6. Risks and Global Supply Chains: What We Know and What We Need to Know
Question: Are global supply chains excessively risky, relative to their benefits?
My takeaway: I want to keep the distinction between a shock and its propagation. Resilience has an opportunity cost: specialization creates gains as well as exposure. A policy argument needs a private–social wedge.
If Yannis asks “What is still missing after this survey?”
The survey helps define questions, but its early-pandemic gaps must be checked against later work. I would investigate recovery dynamics, information quality and incentives rather than repeat its 2021 agenda as new.
Connection: This survey organizes the economic question; Tomlin and base–surge provide operational benchmarks, while later network papers formalize different mechanisms.
Boundary: Review evidence; not an original intervention estimate or a complete 2026 literature census.
Open detailed source note.


7. Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
Question: Do supply links transmit a geographically localized disaster?
My takeaway: The earthquake setting makes indirect economic exposure visible. Both suppliers and customers outside the disaster zone can suffer through the network. Geographic distance is not enough to define an unaffected firm.
If Yannis asks “Is the earthquake a causal experiment for diversification?”
It helps identify exposure to the disaster, not random assignment of sourcing policy. Better-managed firms may both diversify and recover faster. Spillovers also complicate the control group.
Connection: Inoue–Todo simulates propagation on a large network; this paper estimates effects around an actual shock. Guan simulates lockdown scenarios.
Boundary: The local PDF is the December 2016 working paper. Its gross-output propagation estimate must not be relabeled as the published paper’s GDP effect.
Open detailed source note.


8. Trade and Domestic Production Networks
Question: How much foreign exposure passes through domestic firms?
My takeaway: A non-importer can still depend heavily on foreign inputs through domestic suppliers. Allowing links to change is especially important for larger counterfactual trade shocks.
If Yannis asks “Why is this more than an input–output table?”
It uses Belgian firm-to-firm transactions and trade records and models supplier choice. The micro network reveals heterogeneous indirect exposure hidden in sector averages.
Connection: Alfaro–Chor shows direct sourcing shifts; this paper explains why indirect links change their interpretation.
Boundary: Restricted administrative data; model-based foreign-price counterfactuals, not observed responses to every current policy.
Open detailed source note.


9. The Return to Protectionism
Question: Who bears tariffs, and how are gains and losses distributed?
My takeaway: In the 2018 episode, import buyers bore substantial duty-inclusive costs. Gross buyer losses, producer gains, tariff revenue and net real-income effects are different objects.
If Yannis asks “Can I use the estimated pass-through for today’s tariffs?”
Only as evidence from that episode. Pass-through depends on product markets, time horizon and adjustment. I would not assume the 2018 estimate is a universal 2026 parameter.
Connection: Caliendo–Parro is a quantitative tariff/welfare benchmark; Niu studies actual sourcing restructuring; Jain links sourcing to inventory.
Boundary: The consulted version’s $51bn gross loss and $7.2bn net loss are not interchangeable; the net estimate is statistically uncertain.
Open detailed source note.


10. The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
Question: Why do independent sector shocks sometimes fail to average out?
My takeaway: An uneven input–output structure makes some sectors influential through direct and indirect connections. Aggregate risk depends on the distribution of network influence, not simply the number of sectors or links.
If Yannis asks “What is genuinely newer if this was already known in 2012?”
The propagation foundation is older. The newer questions in this list concern link formation, adaptation, private versus social resilience and richer transaction data. I should describe that progression rather than call the whole field new.
Connection: Baqaee–Farhi adds nonlinear response beyond a first-order approximation; Elliott adds essential-input reliability and endogenous investment.
Boundary: An illustrative input–output exercise is not a sufficient-statistic measurement of every observed aggregate fluctuation.
Open detailed source note.


11. Restructuring Global Supply Chains: Navigating Challenges of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
Question: What operating actions did firms actually take during disruption?
My takeaway: Supplier diversification and country diversification are separate. Firms changed supplier portfolios, sourcing volumes and shipment patterns during 2019–2021, with differences across industries.
If Yannis asks “What exactly is observed, and what is inferred?”
The matched sample has 1,533 listed US importers, 4,444 HS6 products and 284,017 firm–product–quarter observations. Shipment size and frequency are observed; exact safety-stock targets, tier-2 changes and causal resilience benefits are not.
Connection: Alfaro–Chor provides the trade picture; Jain provides inventory and recovery outcomes. Together they suggest measuring the consequences of particular actions.
Boundary: Panjiva sea manifests plus Compustat do not cover all firms or transport modes. A published research agenda is not a verified new gap.
Open detailed source note.


12. Managing Global Sourcing: Inventory Performance
Question: How does global sourcing affect inventory investment?
My takeaway: Physical inventory and dollars tied up are different. Longer replenishment can require more units, while cheaper units offset some cost. In the consulted sample the inventory effect dominates; diversification can offset part of it.
If Yannis asks “Are these causal universal percentages?”
No. The local working paper uses matched sea-import and accounting data with simultaneous-equation assumptions. I would explain the mechanism and qualify the sample-specific estimates.
Connection: The recovery paper studies a different outcome and finds diversification associated with slower recovery. This does not contradict a lower inventory burden in a different setting.
Boundary: Pre-COVID public wholesale/retail sample and a 2012 working-paper PDF; not a current all-industry elasticity.
Open detailed source note.


13. On the Value of Mitigation and Contingency Strategies for Managing Supply Chain Disruption Risks
Question: When should a buyer prepare before a disruption versus respond afterward?
My takeaway: Inventory, reliable sourcing and contingent rerouting protect in different ways. The duration and pattern of outages matter, not just average uptime.
If Yannis asks “Why does the same uptime permit different sourcing policies?”
A stock buffer can bridge short failures yet run out during a long failure. A responsive backup depends on available volume flexibility. I have checked the publisher abstract; I would not claim to have verified the full policy theorem.
Connection: Base–surge balances cost and responsiveness to demand; Tomlin explicitly treats supplier disruption. Kopytov moves reliability choice to an economy-wide welfare framework.
Boundary: Abstract-level analysis unless an additional full text is explicitly documented. The single-strategy result has restrictive capacity/flexibility assumptions.
Open detailed source note.


14. Smart Predict, then Optimize
Question: Should training minimize prediction error or the cost of the decision it induces?
My takeaway: An error matters when it changes an action and makes that action costly. SPO changes the learning objective while preserving a predict-then-optimize deployment workflow.
If Yannis asks “Can SPO solve uncertainty about whether a backup actually exists?”
The base framework predicts linear objective coefficients on a known feasible set. Missing capacity or unknown constraints are not automatically covered. I must check that the mathematical representation matches the real uncertainty.
Connection: Ban–Rudin learns feature-dependent inventory actions; Bertsimas–Kallus uses covariates in conditional optimization. ORLM instead produces a formulation/code; OptiGuide supports questions around a solver.
Boundary: Conditional consistency results and numerical evidence do not guarantee superiority under arbitrary distribution shift or uncertain feasibility.
Open detailed source note.


15. Chinese firms are wrapping their supply chains around the globe
Question: How can Chinese production ecosystems expand abroad while direct sourcing shifts?
My takeaway: Factory country, ownership and input origin tell different stories. The article helps me avoid treating every foreign assembly site as an independent production system.
If Yannis asks “Does this prove imports from Vietnam are transshipment?”
No. Actual local production, Chinese ownership and Chinese intermediate inputs can coexist. Transshipment is a separate claim requiring evidence.
Connection: Use alongside Alfaro–Chor’s trade evidence and Niu’s sourcing actions, with clear distinctions in evidentiary strength.
Boundary: Accessible Mint syndicated article and public Substack excerpt; not the paid continuation or a causal academic study.
Open detailed source note.


16. Building an alliance to map global supply networks
Question: What would it take to observe global firm-level supply networks?
My takeaway: VAT, payment and customs records can reveal complementary portions of a network. Connecting national maps is an institutional and measurement problem as well as a technical one.
If Yannis asks “Can we simply download these data?”
Usually not. Administrative and bank microdata require access arrangements. Commercial data may be selective. A firm-level edge also does not reveal the actual part or spare capacity.
Connection: Lee–So–Tang studies the value of a specific demand signal; this article concerns network observability. SPO provides one way to think about decision value.
Boundary: Policy Forum / mapping proposal, not a newly estimated intervention or proof that complete visibility is optimal.
Open detailed source note.


17. Outside the Box: How Globalization Changed from Moving Stuff to Spreading Ideas
Question: How did globalization change from transport integration to fragmented production and ideas?
My takeaway: The historical perspective helps me see operating systems behind trade patterns: transport, coordination, inventory and hidden dependencies develop together.
If Yannis asks “What concrete example would I use?”
The selected chapter’s Riken or BMW coating example shows how an inexpensive upstream input can constrain costly downstream production. I would use it to motivate a question, then turn to empirical or theoretical evidence.
Connection: The Box and Humble Hero explain transport standardization; recent network papers explain mechanisms and consequences more formally.
Boundary: Selected introduction and chapters 14, 19 and 20; not a full reading of the 287-page book or causal verification of its cases.
Open detailed source note.


18. Global supply-chain effects of COVID-19 control measures
Question: How do duration and coordination shape disruption losses?
My takeaway: Recovery depends on connected regions recovering too. A local restart may not restore production if input shortages persist elsewhere.
If Yannis asks “Are the reported losses observed pandemic GDP losses?”
No. They are outcomes of 39 idealized scenarios under the model’s constraints and recovery assumptions. They illustrate sensitivity to duration and spread rather than directly measure a realized causal treatment effect.
Connection: Carvalho studies an actual shock; Inoue simulates firm-network propagation. These are distinct forms of evidence.
Boundary: Early-pandemic scenarios; not a complete epidemiological optimization or a validated forecast for current events.
Open detailed source note.


19. The humble hero: containers have been more important for globalisation than freer trade
Question: How can an operating standard reshape international trade?
My takeaway: Containers reduced handling frictions and improved reliability, making longer production systems easier to coordinate. This reminds me to look beyond small changes in freight prices.
If Yannis asks “Were containers more important than free trade?”
That is the article’s framing of historical research, not a universal ranking I can apply to all periods. Adoption, ports and trade policy changed together.
Connection: Use Levinson for history and formal network/trade papers for mechanisms; read the underlying containerization study before citing its magnitudes.
Boundary: Complete three-page local excerpt; journalism, with the underlying empirical identification not independently checked.
Open detailed source note.

title: Meeting with Yannis: understanding the field
text:
Questions beyond individual papers







If he asks…
My answer at this stage




“Where is the trend?”
In this selection, toward endogenous networks and adaptation, measured operating responses, information/coordination and AI-enabled workflows/infrastructure. That is a qualitative map, not a count of publication growth.


“What is new about AI?”
Prediction-to-decision was already established before LLMs. Formulation, natural-language interaction, task delegation and the supply chain for compute are distinct newer margins to investigate.


“What would make this OM?”
A concrete feasible operating choice, a mechanism explaining its consequences and a strong comparison. A new graph or benchmark accuracy alone might be principally a methods contribution.


“Which topic have you selected?”
None yet. I want to compare adaptation/recovery, information/incentives and AI-related operations, and check data access before narrowing.


“What do these papers prove about AI adoption?”
The methods papers demonstrate specific capabilities; ORLM also includes a small assistance study. They do not jointly establish economy-wide or supply-chain resilience gains from adoption.


“Can we make a policy recommendation?”
Only after defining social welfare and an externality. Buyer cost reduction alone does not justify a subsidy.


“Where would we get data?”

How do firms rewire their input choices when uncertainty increases?

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
text:
My short version
I read this as a warning against measuring resilience only by output volatility. Firms can move toward safer suppliers, reducing volatility but also giving up productivity. In this model that can be an efficient trade-off, rather than a failure to maximize GDP. The timing is important: firms choose a production technique before productivity shocks are known. Their decisions then reshape both the weights and the links in the network (PDF pp. 1–3). This gives a different explanation for network change from the bargaining externality in Acemoglu and Tahbaz-Salehi.

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
text:
How the paper gets there
The model has competitive firms, a risk-averse representative household and technique choices that change input shares. It characterizes an efficient equilibrium. A basic U.S. calibration uses 37 BEA sectors, 1948–2020. Additional firm-level evidence uses Compustat/stock volatility and FactSet links: riskier suppliers are more likely to lose relationships. The IV exercises address endogeneity but depend on the instruments' exclusion restrictions. Stock volatility is a proxy for uncertainty, not a direct measure of delivery failure (PDF pp. 31–36).

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
section: Why I am keeping it for an OM project
text:
Why I am keeping it for an OM project
For a firm-level OM question, I would separate expected cost, disruption risk and the time needed to qualify a replacement. How much should a buyer pay for stability when switching takes months and risk estimates are noisy? An interesting outcome is the cost of stability, not just whether a firm diversifies. I could compare a static safe-supplier choice with a dynamic policy that learns and keeps a backup option.

title: Endogenous Production Networks Under Supply Chain Uncertainty
section: What I still need to be careful about
text:
What I still need to be careful about
The calibration is deliberately stylized and explains only part of network variation. One-year technique adjustment and Cobb–Douglas structure are strong restrictions. I should not read a fall in expected GDP as a fall in welfare. Nor should I assume that the model's efficient flight to safety describes every real supply chain (PDF pp. 32–34).
